lessons.title: Soil Testing and pH Adjustment for Cabbage
lessons.body:
Cabbage grows best in soil with a pH between 6.0 and 6.8. If your soil is too acidic (pH below 6.0), cabbage cannot take up nutrients properly, and you will see poor head formation. If it is too alkaline (above 7.5), you may see yellowing leaves and stunted growth. The first step is to test your soil. You can buy a simple soil test kit from an agro-dealer for about $10â$20. These kits usually test pH and sometimes nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. For a more accurate result, send a soil sample to your local agricultural extension office. To take a sample, dig 15 cm deep in 10â15 spots across your field, mix the soil in a clean bucket, and take about 500 g of the mixed soil. Test before planting, ideally 2â3 months before, so you have time to adjust.

If your soil is too acidic (pH below 6.0), apply agricultural lime (calcium carbonate) or dolomitic lime. The amount needed depends on your soil type. On sandy soil, apply 1â2 tonnes per hectare to raise pH by 0.5â1.0 unit. On clay soil, you may need 2â4 tonnes per hectare. Spread lime evenly and mix it into the top 15 cm of soil. Lime works slowly, so apply at least 4â6 weeks before planting. If your soil is too alkaline (pH above 7.5), add elemental sulfur or gypsum. Apply 200â500 kg per hectare of elemental sulfur, or 1â2 tonnes per hectare of gypsum. Mix into the soil and wait 4â6 weeks. Organic matter like compost or well-rotted manure also helps buffer pH and improve soil structure.

After adjusting, retest the soil to confirm the pH is in the right range. If you cannot afford a lab test, you can use a simple pH meter or litmus paper. Remember, cabbage is sensitive to pH, so do not skip this step. In many African soils, acidity is a common problem due to heavy rains and continuous farming. Adding lime not only raises pH but also supplies calcium and magnesium, which cabbage needs for strong heads. Keep records of your test results and lime applications so you can adjust in future seasons.

lessons.title: Tillage and Seedbed Preparation Techniques
lessons.body:
Cabbage needs a fine, loose seedbed for good root growth and uniform head development. Start by clearing the field of weeds, rocks, and crop residues. If you have a hoe or ox-drawn plough, till the soil to a depth of 20â30 cm. This breaks up hardpan and allows roots to penetrate deeply. In most African smallholder farms, hand hoeing is common, but it is labour-intensive. If you can access a tractor or power tiller, one pass is usually enough, but avoid over-tilling, which destroys soil structure and causes compaction.

After primary tillage, break up large clods with a rake or hoe. The seedbed should be level and fine, like a garden bed. Cabbage seeds are small, so a fine seedbed ensures good seed-to-soil contact and uniform germination. If you are transplanting seedlings, the bed should be firm enough so that seedlings stand upright. Prepare raised beds if your area has heavy rains or poor drainage. Raised beds should be 15â20 cm high and 1â1.2 m wide, with paths of 30â40 cm between beds. This improves drainage and makes weeding and harvesting easier.

For direct seeding, sow seeds 1â2 cm deep in rows 45â60 cm apart. For transplanting, start seedlings in a nursery bed and transplant when they have 4â6 true leaves, about 3â4 weeks after sowing. Space plants 45â60 cm apart within rows and 60â75 cm between rows, depending on the variety. Closer spacing gives smaller heads; wider spacing gives larger heads. After transplanting, firm the soil around the roots and water immediately. A well-prepared seedbed saves water, reduces weeds, and gives your cabbage a strong start. In dry areas, prepare beds before the rains to capture moisture. In wet areas, ensure beds are raised to avoid waterlogging.

lessons.title: Organic Matter Incorporation and Composting
lessons.body:
Organic matter is the backbone of healthy cabbage soil. It improves soil structure, holds water, and feeds beneficial microbes. In Africa, you can use cattle manure, goat manure, poultry litter, or crop residues like maize stalks and bean haulms. Fresh manure can burn plants, so compost it first. To make compost, build a pile of alternating layers of green materials (fresh grass, kitchen scraps) and brown materials (dry leaves, straw, maize cobs). Add a handful of wood ash or a little old manure to speed up decomposition. Keep the pile as moist as a squeezed sponge and turn it every 2â3 weeks. In 6â8 weeks, you will have dark, crumbly compost that smells earthy.

Apply compost or well-rotted manure at 10â20 tonnes per hectare (about 1â2 kg per square metre) before planting. Spread it evenly and mix it into the top 15 cm of soil. If you have limited manure, concentrate it in the planting holes. For each planting hole, mix one handful (about 100 g) of compost or manure with the soil before transplanting. This gives each cabbage plant a nutrient boost. You can also make compost tea by soaking a sack of compost in water for 24â48 hours, then use the liquid as a foliar feed every 2 weeks.

In addition to compost, consider planting green manures like cowpeas, lablab, or mucuna in the off-season. These legumes fix nitrogen from the air and add organic matter when ploughed under. Sow them after harvest and plough them in before they flower. This is a cheap way to improve soil fertility. Avoid burning crop residues; instead, incorporate them into the soil or use them as mulch. Mulching with dry grass or straw around cabbage plants conserves moisture, suppresses weeds, and adds organic matter as it decomposes. Remember, building organic matter takes time, but it pays off with healthier cabbage and higher yields.

lessons.title: Fertilizer Selection and Application Rates
lessons.body:
Cabbage is a heavy feeder. It needs nitrogen (N) for leaf growth, phosphorus (P) for root development, and potassium (K) for head formation. A soil test will tell you exactly what your soil lacks, but if you cannot test, use a balanced fertilizer like NPK 10-10-10 or 12-24-12 at planting. Apply 200â300 kg per hectare (about 20â30 g per plant) in a band 10 cm away from the plant base, or broadcast and incorporate before planting. Do not let fertilizer touch the stems, as it can burn them.

About 3â4 weeks after transplanting, side-dress with a nitrogen-rich fertilizer like urea (46-0-0) or calcium ammonium nitrate (CAN 27% N). Apply 100â150 kg per hectare (10â15 g per plant) by placing it in a ring around each plant, 10â15 cm from the stem. Repeat every 2â3 weeks until heads start to form. For a 1-hectare field, you may need 300â400 kg of urea in total, split into 2â3 applications. If you use organic sources, poultry manure is rich in nitrogen; apply 2â3 tonnes per hectare. Wood ash is a good source of potassium; apply 500â1000 kg per hectare.

Foliar feeds can correct quick deficiencies. Spray a solution of 20 g urea per litre of water on the leaves early in the morning or late evening. You can also use commercial foliar fertilizers with micronutrients like boron and zinc, which cabbage needs for proper head development. Always follow label instructions. Over-fertilizing with nitrogen can cause leafy growth with loose heads and increase pest problems. Under-fertilizing gives small, pale heads. Split applications are better than one large dose because they match the plant's needs over time. Keep a record of what you apply and when, so you can improve next season.

lessons.title: Nutrient Deficiency Symptoms and Corrections
lessons.body:
Cabbage plants show clear signs when they lack nutrients. Nitrogen deficiency causes older leaves to turn pale green and then yellow, starting from the tips and moving inward. The whole plant looks stunted, and heads are small. To correct, side-dress with urea or CAN at 100â150 kg per hectare, or spray a 2% urea solution (20 g per litre) on leaves. Phosphorus deficiency makes leaves dark green with a purple tinge, especially on the undersides, and roots are weak. Correct by applying NPK 12-24-12 at planting, or add bone meal or rock phosphate at 200â300 kg per hectare.

Potassium deficiency shows as yellowing and browning at the leaf margins, starting on older leaves. The leaf edges may dry up and curl. Heads are loose and do not store well. Apply potassium chloride (muriate of potash, 0-0-60) at 100â150 kg per hectare, or wood ash at 500â1000 kg per hectare. Calcium deficiency causes tip burn, where the inner leaves turn brown and die. This often happens in acidic soils or when watering is irregular. Lime your soil to pH 6.5 and water consistently. Magnesium deficiency causes yellowing between the veins of older leaves, which may turn reddish-purple. Apply dolomitic lime or Epsom salt (magnesium sulfate) at 50â100 kg per hectare.

Boron deficiency causes hollow stems and brown, corky patches on the head. Apply borax at 10â20 kg per hectare, or use a foliar spray with boron. Zinc deficiency gives small, narrow leaves with yellow spots. Spray zinc sulfate at 5 g per litre. Always confirm the deficiency before treating. If you are unsure, ask your extension officer. Correcting deficiencies early gives better heads. Remember, a balanced soil test is the best guide. Over-application can also be harmful, so follow recommended rates.

lessons.title: Soil Conservation Practices for Cabbage Fields
lessons.body:
Cabbage fields are often on slopes or in areas with heavy rains, so soil erosion is a real threat. Losing topsoil means losing nutrients and organic matter, which reduces yields. To conserve soil, start by planting cover crops like cowpeas, lablab, or sweet potatoes between cabbage rows or after harvest. These cover the soil, reduce raindrop impact, and their roots hold soil in place. You can also use mulch from dry grass, straw, or maize stover. Apply a 5â10 cm layer around cabbage plants, leaving a small gap around the stem to prevent rot. Mulch reduces erosion, conserves moisture, and suppresses weeds.

On sloping land, construct contour barriers. Dig trenches or ridges along the contour lines, about 20â30 cm deep and 30â40 cm wide, spaced 10â15 m apart. These slow down runoff and trap soil. You can also plant vetiver grass or napier grass along contours as living barriers. These deep-rooted grasses hold the soil and can be cut for fodder. If you have a steep slope, consider making bench terraces, though this is labour-intensive. Even simple measures like planting across the slope instead of up and down can reduce erosion by half.

Maintain soil organic matter by adding compost or manure every season. Avoid leaving soil bare; always keep it covered with crops or mulch. Rotate cabbage with cereals like maize or sorghum, and with legumes. This breaks pest cycles and improves soil health. Do not burn crop residues; instead, incorporate them or use them as mulch. Reduce tillage to minimum; excessive ploughing destroys soil structure and makes it vulnerable to erosion. If you use a plough, plough along the contour, not up and down. Finally, plant windbreaks like grevillea or casuarina trees on the edges of your field to reduce wind erosion. These practices will keep your soil productive for years.

quiz.q: What is the ideal soil pH range for cabbage?
quiz.explanation: Cabbage grows best in slightly acidic to neutral soil with pH 6.0â6.8.

quiz.q: Which material is commonly used to raise soil pH?
quiz.explanation: Agricultural lime (calcium carbonate) is used to increase pH in acidic soils.

quiz.q: How deep should you take soil samples for testing?
quiz.explanation: A depth of 15 cm is standard for soil testing as it represents the root zone for most crops.

quiz.q: What is the recommended amount of lime for sandy soil to raise pH by 0.5â1.0 unit?
quiz.explanation: Sandy soil requires 1â2 tonnes per hectare of lime to raise pH by 0.5â1.0 unit.

quiz.q: How long before planting should lime be applied?
quiz.explanation: Lime reacts slowly, so it should be applied 4â6 weeks before planting.

quiz.q: What is the primary purpose of tillage?
options: B) To break up soil and prepare seedbed
quiz.explanation: Tillage loosens soil, breaks hardpan, and creates a fine seedbed for planting.

quiz.q: What is the recommended depth for primary tillage?
quiz.explanation: Tilling to 20â30 cm depth allows deep root penetration and better drainage.

quiz.q: Why are raised beds recommended in areas with heavy rains?
quiz.explanation: Raised beds prevent waterlogging by improving drainage in wet conditions.

quiz.q: What is the ideal spacing for cabbage transplants?
quiz.explanation: Spacing of 45â60 cm between plants allows proper head development.

quiz.q: When should cabbage seedlings be transplanted?
options: B) When they have 4â6 true leaves
quiz.explanation: Transplant when seedlings have 4â6 true leaves, usually 3â4 weeks after sowing.

quiz.q: Which of these is a green manure crop?
quiz.explanation: Cowpea is a legume that fixes nitrogen and can be ploughed under as green manure.

quiz.q: How long does it take to make compost?
quiz.explanation: With regular turning and proper moisture, compost is ready in 6â8 weeks.

quiz.q: What is the recommended application rate of compost or manure per hectare?
quiz.explanation: Apply 10â20 tonnes per hectare of compost or well-rotted manure before planting.

quiz.q: Which material is a good source of potassium?
quiz.explanation: Wood ash is rich in potassium and can be used to correct potassium deficiency.

quiz.q: What is the main nutrient needed for cabbage leaf growth?
quiz.explanation: Nitrogen promotes leafy growth, which is essential for cabbage.

quiz.q: What is a common side-dressing fertilizer for cabbage?
quiz.explanation: Urea (46-0-0) is a nitrogen-rich fertilizer commonly used for side-dressing.

quiz.q: How much urea per plant is recommended for side-dressing?
quiz.explanation: Apply 10â15 g of urea per plant in a ring around the base.

quiz.q: What is the danger of over-fertilizing with nitrogen?
options: B) Loose heads and pest problems
quiz.explanation: Excess nitrogen causes excessive leaf growth with loose heads and attracts pests.

quiz.q: What deficiency causes tip burn in cabbage?
quiz.explanation: Calcium deficiency leads to tip burn, where inner leaves turn brown and die.

quiz.q: Which nutrient deficiency shows purple tinge on leaves?
quiz.explanation: Phosphorus deficiency often causes purple discoloration, especially on leaf undersides.

quiz.q: What is a symptom of potassium deficiency in cabbage?
quiz.explanation: Potassium deficiency causes browning and drying at leaf margins, starting on older leaves.

quiz.q: How can you correct magnesium deficiency?
quiz.explanation: Epsom salt (magnesium sulfate) provides magnesium to correct deficiency.

quiz.q: Which micronutrient deficiency causes hollow stems in cabbage?
quiz.explanation: Boron deficiency leads to hollow stems and brown corky patches on heads.

quiz.q: What is the best way to confirm a nutrient deficiency?
quiz.explanation: A soil test provides accurate diagnosis of nutrient deficiencies.

quiz.q: Which practice helps conserve soil on slopes?
quiz.explanation: Contour barriers slow runoff and trap soil on sloping land.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of mulching cabbage fields?
options: B) Conserves moisture and reduces erosion
quiz.explanation: Mulch conserves soil moisture, suppresses weeds, and reduces erosion.

quiz.q: Which grass is commonly used as a living barrier for soil conservation?
quiz.explanation: Vetiver grass has deep roots and is effective for contour barriers.

quiz.q: Why is crop rotation important for cabbage?
options: B) It breaks pest cycles and improves soil
quiz.explanation: Rotating with cereals and legumes breaks pest cycles and improves soil health.

quiz.q: What should you do with crop residues?
quiz.explanation: Incorporating or mulching residues adds organic matter and protects soil.

quiz.q: What is the recommended spacing for contour barriers?
quiz.explanation: Contour barriers should be spaced 10â15 m apart on sloping land.
